title: The flood (Genesis 7)
hookLine: the fountains of the deep break open, and God remembers Noah
tomorrow: The dove and the olive leaf

cards: Go back to the very first page. Darkness on the face of the deep, waters everywhere. Then God divides them: a dome to hold the waters above, seas gathered so dry land can appear.
Creation, in Genesis, is partly a story of water being given its place. Now, in chapter seven, the story runs that film backwards.

The waters come back, up from below, down from above, and the dry land disappears, as if the world is being unmade. And floating on all of it, inside a wooden box, are Noah, his family, and the animals.

teach.h: THE FOUNTAINS OF THE DEEP BROKEN UP.
teach.b: Here's how the King James Bible tells it: "the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened."

The deep from verse two of the Bible, and the waters above the dome from day nine, both let loose at once. Rain for forty days and forty nights. The waters rise over the mountains, and stay for a hundred and fifty days.
Two small details are worth knowing. First, the animals. Two by two is the well-known version.

teach.h: TWO BY TWO, AND BY SEVENS.
teach.b: But chapter seven also tells Noah to take the clean animals, and the birds, by sevens. Both are in the text.
Second, after everyone is inside, there's this: "and the LORD shut him in." Noah doesn't close the door. God does.
Then the long wait, in the dark, with no land anywhere. And at the turn, the first verse of the next chapter: "And God remembered Noah."

teach.h: ZAKHAR: TO REMEMBER IS TO ACT.
teach.b: In Hebrew, zakhar, to remember. It doesn't mean God had forgotten. Here, God's remembering is the hinge.
Right after it, a wind passes over the earth, like the Spirit over the waters at the start, and the waters begin to go down.
Christians read the flood in different ways: some as a worldwide event, some as a regional flood remembered in a great story, some as a story whose truth is about God and people more than geology.
Other ancient peoples told flood stories too.
However it's read, the text turns on three words: God remembered Noah.

how: Some churches pray for those in trouble by name each week, and the first letter of Peter links the flood to baptism, so some churches read the story at the Easter Vigil and recall it in baptism prayers.

a storm that ends when Noah prays for help

games.q: you're inside the ark. the rain has stopped, but there's water everywhere and no land. a hundred and fifty days. what's the turning point in the story?
o: Noah opens the door to look.
games.why: "and God remembered Noah," and a wind passes over the earth, like the Spirit over the waters on the first page.

practice: Think of someone who's in over their head right now, grief, illness, debt, a long dark wait with no land in sight, and picture them wherever they are this evening.
Hold them in mind the way the story says God remembered Noah, a remembering that leads somewhere. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: The flood. The waters of the first page let loose again, the world almost unmade, and in the middle, the turn: God remembered Noah.
